who: People reading in a second language
Deaf people whose first language is sign language
takeaways: There is a way to find the specific meaning of words or phrases used in an unusual or restricted way, including idioms and jargon.
Idioms like “ballpark figure” and jargon like “escrow” or “sprint” can make no sense when read literally or translated.
This is Level AAA. You can meet it with a definition in the text, a link to a glossary, or a definitions panel.
It is a content task, but designers decide where definitions live and how people reach them: inline, in a tooltip people can open, or on a glossary page.
failures: Product jargon like “workspace seat” with no explanation anywhere
Idioms such as “touch base” in help text
Definitions shown only on mouse hover
check: Highlight every term in your copy that a newcomer might not know, or that means something special in your product.
For each, check there is a definition people can reach by keyboard, touch and screen reader.
Replace idioms with plain words where you can, so fewer definitions are needed.

quiz.question: A budgeting app’s alert says “You’re in the red this month.” Some readers use translation tools, which turn it into “you are in the color red”. What meets 3.1.3?
options: Make “in the red” bold so it stands out
Rewrite it as “You have spent more than your budget”, or link the idiom to a definition
Show the alert in red so the meaning is obvious
quiz.why: Read literally, an idiom means something else. Plain words remove the problem, and where the idiom stays, a definition meets the rule. Red text adds a color-only cue, which 1.4.1 rules out.

spec: List the terms that need definitions and write each definition.
Show how each definition is reached: inline text, a toggle or a glossary link.
Make sure definition toggles work with keyboard and touch, and say how they are announced.
review: Would someone new to this industry understand every word here?
Which phrases would make no sense if translated word for word?
Where does someone go if they do not know what this means?
tradeoff: Some jargon is precise and the right word. Keep it, and define it. Remove idioms and jargon that are only habit, since a plain word needs no definition.
system: Provide a definition component for inline terms and a shared glossary that content teams can link to.
pitch: Every word customers do not understand turns into a support call. A glossary and plain language cost less.
